catalog_quote: [p.5] Tone elements are binary H[igh] and L[ow]. Syllables may be H, L, <HL>, or <LH>, rarely <LHL>. Stems and words may be {H}, {L}, {HL}, {LH}, or {LHL}, with the tone elements spread out over the relevant syllables. There are no lexical tone oppositions among verbs, and only marginal oppositions among adjectives, but nouns may be lexically /HL/, /LH/, or /L/. The general pattern is that at most one syllable in a word is H-toned, so the tonal system has a resemblance to pitch-accent systems that have at most one accented syllable and allow unaccented words. [p.27] In the absence of an elaborated stress/accent system, the distinction between elitics [sic, so printed] and particles is not clearcut. [p.29] The distribution of H-tones suggests the possibility of an accentual analysis, with nonfinal accent (H-tone) in (24a), final accent in (24b), and no accent in (24c). ... One attractive option would be initial accent (hence Cv́v, Cv́Cv, Cv́vCv, Cv́CvCv, etc.) followed by Rightward H-Spreading through the penult where needed (Cv́v́Cv, Cv́Cv́Cv). ... In polysyllabic words, the peak of pitch and intensity in e.g. an H.(H.)H.L syllable sequence is just before the tone break, giving the impression of an M.(M.)H.L sequence. In an accentual model, we could formalize this as an accent on that syllable, perhaps after Rightward H-Movement from a starting point at the left edge.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bunoge is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with no elaborated stress/accent system; word prosody is carried by lexical/grammatical tone melodies (/HL/, /LH/, /L/ for nouns), typically with at most one H per word (pitch accent-like). Phonetically, in H..H.L words the pitch-and-intensity peak falls on the last H syllable, immediately before the H-to-L tone break; Heath floats but does not adopt an accentual reanalysis (initial accent plus rightward H-spreading; /LH/ = final accent; /L/ = unaccented).
new_statements.exceptions: sec. 3.1.2 (p.11): no metrical weakening of medial syllables in CvCvCv; weak (raising/syncope) position is stem-final vowel before certain suffixes. sec. 4.6.1.4 (p.86): before numeral '2' nouns become tonally flat with H plural -gé, producing strings of H syllables that 'go against the pitch accent tendencies of the rest of the language'. Monosyllabic /HL/ and /LH/ nouns have merged (constraint against rising tone on Cv).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word (noun stems and their tone melodies; clitic diagnosis). The intensity-peak remark is an impressionistic phonetic observation on polysyllabic words, not an instrumental result. Tone overlays (tonosyntax) can replace lexical melodies at phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bunoge (buno1241) as spoken in Sangou and Boudou villages (western Dogon, near Goundaka), data mainly from one Sangou speaker (2012, 2017) plus Boudou texts (2015). Earlier names: 'budu tagu' (Plungian & Tembine 1994), 'Korandabo' (Hochstetler et al. 2004, actually a greeting). Note the PuRe metadata record mislabels the ISO subject as 'dym Yanda Dom'; the file itself is the Bunoge grammar.

sources.note: Tone language (binary H/L; noun melodies /HL/, /LH/, /L/). No dedicated stress section. p.5: at most one H syllable per word, 'resemblance to pitch accent systems'; p.11 (3.1.2 Metrical structure): no tendency for medial syllable of CvCvCv to weaken; p.27: 'In the absence of an elaborated stress/accent system..'; p.29: peak of pitch and intensity in H.(H.)H.L words is on the syllable just before the tone break, accentual analysis (initial accent + rightward H-spreading) floated but not adopted; p.86: strings of H syllables 'go against the pitch accent tendencies of the rest of the language'.

sources.note: A 6-page comparative note on Dogon lexical tone melodies (binary H/L; syllables H, L, <HL>, <LH>, rarely <LHL>; verbs /H/ vs /LH/ in eastern Dogon, partly predictable from initial obstruent voicing). For Bunoge it states only that, as in the other southwestern languages and Tiranige, all verb forms have tones predictable from the inflectional category, i.e. verbs have no lexical tone melodies. No Bunoge noun data.

sources.note: Dogon NP tonosyntax arose from (a) a right-headed prosodic pattern in noun-modifier sequences, (b) loss of numeral classifiers, and (c) transfer of tones from possessors to following possessums; the resulting tone-overlay system is stable and unique to Dogon. Bunoge-specific content unseen.
